summary: At just 5.7 square miles, Beverly Hills packs a median home value exceeding $2 million into a footprint smaller than many regional parks — yet it functions as a genuine employment center, not merely a residential enclave, with entertainment, luxury retail, hospitality, and professional services generating enough economic activity that the daytime population dwarfs the roughly 32,000 residents. The city sits where the flat basin of the Los Angeles Westside tilts upward into the Santa Monica Mountains, so the northern residential streets climb into canyons with genuine ridgeline views while the southern flats around the commercial triangle stay walkable and gridded. That dual geography means evening walks range from steep, winding canyon roads to level strolls past Rodeo Drive storefronts. Affordability, though, is stark: the median home price represents more than fifteen times the median household income of roughly $128,000, and even median rent at $2,805 consumes over a quarter of that gross figure. Property crime runs notably high at 4,818 per 100,000 — heavily weighted toward larceny at 3,536 — consistent with a commercial district drawing millions of visitors annually. Daily highs average 75°F with nearly ten hours of sunshine year-round, meaning overcast days genuinely surprise. Beverly Hills is, in essence, a small city that operates at the economic intensity of a much larger one, with a cost of entry that the income data alone doesn't explain.
